preamble: Shift of the palatalized alveolar nasal [nʲ] to a true palatal (alveolo-palatal) nasal [ɲ], moving the primary constriction from the alveolar ridge to the hard palate. In West Slavic, the soft [nʲ] that arose before front vowels became palatal: Polish ń/ni and Slovak and Czech ň continue Common Slavic soft n, whereas Russian keeps a palatalized alveolar [nʲ] (небо [ˈnʲebə]). Czech later depalatalized n before e, so the palatal survives there mainly before i and as written ň.

examples.from: Proto-Slavic *nebo 'sky' with soft [nʲ] before the front vowel (cf. Russian небо [ˈnʲebə])
examples.note: Polish soft n became the alveolo-palatal nasal spelled ń / ni.

examples.from: Proto-Slavic *dьnь 'day' (final soft n before the front jer)
examples.note: After the loss of the final jer the palatal nasal stands word-finally, spelled ń.
Slovak n before e is the palatal nasal ň [ɲ], unlike Czech nebe [ˈnɛbɛ].
Word-final soft n surfaces as ň [ɲ].
In the 13th–14th-century depalatalization, softened consonants either merged with hard ones or became palatal ď, ť, ň; n before i became ň.
Written ni but pronounced with palatal [ɲ].
